title: Mediation Act ss. 4–6 — Pre-litigation mediation & Non-mediatable disputes (Mediation ss. 4-6)

content.overview: Sections 4 to 6 of the Mediation Act, 2023 deal with the mediation agreement, pre-litigation mediation, and disputes not fit for mediation. A mediation agreement is a written agreement by or between parties, and anyone claiming through them, to submit existing or future disputes to mediation. It may be a clause or a separate agreement, and writing includes a signed document, an exchange including electronic communications under the Information Technology Act, 2000, or pleadings in which the agreement is alleged and not denied. Parties may agree to mediate a dispute arising under an agreement whether the agreement is made before or after the dispute. Section 5 provides for pre-litigation mediation, defined as mediation before a suit or civil or commercial proceeding is filed in a court or notified tribunal. Section 6 bars mediation of disputes in the indicative list in the First Schedule, with a proviso that a court may still refer a dispute relating to a compoundable offence, including a compoundable matrimonial offence pending between the parties, if it considers that appropriate.
content.glance: Mediation Act ss. 4–6 — Pre-litigation mediation & Non-mediatable disputes (Mediation ss. 4-6). Complete ADR treatise with statutory deconstruction, examples, verified authorities, forum analysis and chamber drafting.
content.study: Test writing and parties under s. 4 before discussing process. Use s. 5 for the pre-filing route and s. 6 plus the First Schedule for subject-matter fitness. Do not treat the First Schedule bar as absolute where the compoundable-offence proviso applies, and do not treat the proviso as a licence to mediate non-compoundable offences.

cases.issue: When should a court refer parties to arbitration and which disputes are non-arbitrable?

cases.facts: The dispute concerned unilateral appointment power vested in an interested party.
cases.issue: Whether a person interested in the outcome may unilaterally appoint the sole arbitrator.
cases.ratioDecidendi: A person rendered ineligible to act as arbitrator cannot control the appointment process in a manner that creates justifiable bias.
cases.holding: The unilateral appointment mechanism was held invalid in the circumstances.
cases.relevance: Use for independence, impartiality and appointment challenges.

learningObjectives: Apply the writing and form tests for a mediation agreement in s. 4.
Describe pre-litigation mediation under s. 5 without collapsing it into court-referred mediation under s. 7.
Apply the First Schedule bar in s. 6 and the compoundable-offence proviso.
enhancement.definition: Section 4 defines and formalises the mediation agreement. Section 5 provides the pre-litigation mediation route. Section 6 excludes First Schedule matters from mediation, subject to the court's proviso for compoundable offences including compoundable matrimonial offences.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Mediation under the Act starts from a written agreement or a statutory pre-litigation or court-referred route, and it cannot be conducted for a dispute in the indicative list in the First Schedule except as the s. 6 proviso allows.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Mediation Act, 2023, ss. 4, 5 and 6 and the First Schedule; writing includes electronic form under the Information Technology Act, 2000; court reference is s. 7 and is outside this topic except as a distinction.
essentialIngredients: Agreement by or between parties, including persons claiming through them
Writing: signed document, exchange of communications including electronic form, or undenied pleading
Clause or separate agreement; may cover disputes that have arisen or may arise
International mediation agreement confined to commercial disputes as defined
Pre-litigation mediation is the s. 5 process before filing
First Schedule matter excluded unless the compoundable-offence proviso applies
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 4(1) to (4) is a form statute. A mediation clause incorporated by reference is a mediation agreement if the host agreement is in writing and the reference makes the clause part of it. Section 4(5) allows a submission made before or after the dispute arises. Section 4(6) narrows international mediation agreements to commercial disputes. Section 5 must be read with the definition of pre-litigation mediation: it is the process for settlement before a civil or commercial suit or proceeding is filed. It is distinct from a court or tribunal reference under s. 7. Section 6(1) incorporates the First Schedule as an indicative list of matters not fit for mediation. The proviso is narrow: a court may refer compoundable offences, including compoundable matrimonial offences pending between the parties, if it deems that appropriate. Whether a particular notified commencement date has brought ss. 4 to 6 into force must be checked against the Central Government notification under s. 1(3); this note does not assert that every subsection is in force on every date.
examples: A services contract contains a mediation clause; a later dispute is within s. 4.
One party alleges a mediation agreement in the plaint and the other does not deny it; s. 4(3)(c) writing is met.
Parties attempt settlement of a commercial claim before filing; that is the s. 5 route, not a s. 7 reference.
A non-compoundable criminal prosecution is said to be mediated under s. 6; the proviso does not cover it.

keyTakeaways: A mediation agreement must be in writing in one of the s. 4(3) modes.
It may be a clause or a separate agreement and may be pre-dispute or post-dispute.
Pre-litigation mediation is the before-filing route in s. 5.
First Schedule matters are not fit for mediation, subject to the compoundable-offence proviso.
